analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA and the Army Corps from enforcing the Clean Water Act rule defining which streams and wetlands are protected.
analysis.headline: Despite 186 cosponsors, the bill never received a House vote and died in a Transportation and Infrastructure subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit the EPA and the Army Corps of Engineers from issuing or enforcing the 2015 "Waters of the United States" rule, which clarifies which small streams, wetlands, and other waters are covered by the Clean Water Act and therefore require permits before they can be polluted or filled. It would also ban the agencies from using any "substantially similar" rule in the future, withdraw an existing rule clarifying which farm conservation practices are exempt from permits, and require a lengthy consultation with state and local officials before any replacement rule could be proposed. The practical effect is to block a rule that would extend federal water pollution protections to smaller streams and wetlands, which farm, development, and energy interests had strongly opposed.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be farm operators, real estate developers, homebuilders, and mining and energy companies that discharge into or fill small streams and wetlands. Without the Waters of the United States rule, many of those waters would fall outside federal Clean Water Act permitting, so these businesses would avoid the cost and delay of obtaining pollution discharge or dredge-and-fill permits. Landowners would also face less federal oversight over how they use wet areas on their property.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Army Corps and EPA from developing, finalizing, adopting, implementing, or enforcing the proposed "Definition of Waters of the United States" rule, and bans them from using it or any substantially similar rule as the basis for any Clean Water Act decision.
Makes any use of the prohibited rule or guidance grounds for having the resulting rule, decision, or enforcement action thrown out in court.
Requires the agencies to withdraw an interpretive rule about exemptions for certain agricultural conservation practices from permitting.

Requires a joint consultation with state and local officials, a consensus requirement, and a draft and final report process before any new regulatory proposal on the scope of covered waters, with a public comment period of at least 180 days.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on the people who rely on small streams and wetlands for clean water. Many seasonal and headwater streams feed the rivers and reservoirs that supply drinking water to downstream communities, and wetlands filter pollution and absorb floods. Leaving those waters outside federal Clean Water Act permitting would shift the burden of polluted drinking water, degraded fishing and recreation, and flood damage onto downstream residents and local governments, while making it harder to hold upstream polluters accountable.
analysis.who_pays_short: Downstream communities and drinking water consumers

drawbacks.text: The bill would block the entire rulemaking rather than amend it, so any parts of the rule that addressed real gaps in protection for small streams and wetlands would be blocked along with parts that businesses found burdensome.
It would bar not just the specific rule but any "substantially similar" proposal, limiting the agencies' ability to craft a narrower version that addressed critics' concerns.

It would withdraw the interpretive rule that identified which farm conservation practices were exempt from permitting, replacing a clear safe harbor for farmers with more uncertainty about their obligations.

The bill's own consultation process requires consensus among federal agencies and state and local officials before any recommendation can be included, a high bar that could make a replacement rule difficult to produce at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core effect is to stop a rule that would expand federal protection for small streams and wetlands, which supporters argue reduced permitting costs and uncertainty for landowners and respected state authority over land and water. The tradeoff is that waters which had been clearly protected would lose that protection, and downstream communities would bear more of the cost of pollution with no federal backstop. The bill would replace the rule with a consultation process that requires full consensus before any recommendation, meaning a replacement might not arrive at all. For ordinary people who drink water sourced from these streams, the bill offers little direct benefit and removes an existing protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then sent to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, where it sat and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Paul Gosar introduced the bill in the House on January 28, 2015, and it was referred to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The bill attracted 186 cosponsors, 183 Republicans and 3 Democrats, showing broad House support on the bill's face.
The day after introduction, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and no further action was taken for the remainder of the 114th Congress.
The bill never received a committee markup, a House floor vote, or action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that would have faced new Clean Water Act permitting requirements under the Waters of the United States rule are better off, since the bill died and the rule's protections were never statutorily blocked by this bill, though the rule remained contested in the courts.

for.name: Paul Gosar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 186 cosponsors.

for.name: Agricultural and development interests
for.role: Opponents of the Waters of the United States rule
for.what_they_did: Organized publicly against the rule the bill would block, supplying much of the political backing for the bill.

against.name: Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup on the bill; the bill was referred to subcommittee and stayed there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 186 cosponsors included 183 Republicans and only 3 Democrats, making support heavily one-sided by party.

industries.note: The bill would block a rule that would have required permits for discharges into many small streams, ditches, and wetlands on farmland, saving farmers from permitting costs and enforcement risk. The savings come at the expense of downstream water quality, since runoff from those operations would face less federal oversight.

Developers would avoid dredge-and-fill permits for building on or near wetlands and small streams, lowering project costs. The tradeoff is loss of wetlands that filter water and absorb flooding for nearby communities.

Companies that discharge mining waste or drilling wastewater into small streams would face fewer permitting hurdles and less enforcement exposure. The cost of that easing falls on downstream water users.

industries.industry: Municipal water utilities and downstream water consumers
industries.note: Utilities and the communities they serve would lose federal protection for the upstream streams and wetlands that feed their water supplies, raising the cost of treating polluted source water. Their interest in clean upstream water runs directly against what the bill would do.
